content.text:
Welcome

This course is for learners who can use files and a web browser but may never have programmed before. In about 30 hours you will progress from a first Python expression to a small, evidence-based data analysis.

By the end, you can

  • read, run, test, and modify basic Python;
  • use conditions, loops, collections, and functions;
  • load, inspect, clean, and summarise CSV data with pandas;
  • make an appropriate chart with matplotlib;
  • state a conclusion and a limitation in your own words;
  • use AI assistance without surrendering verification or judgment.

Study cycle

Read → Type → Run → Change → Explain. Do not only read code. Type it, predict the result, run it, change one input, and explain the new result. A local Python installation is enough. Internet access and an AI account are optional.

How learning checks work

All 12 learning checks are required for course completion, but they are not one-time exams.

You may try each check as many times as needed, and your highest score is kept. A score of 90% completes the check.

A lower score does not mean that you have failed the course. It identifies what to practise next. Read the feedback, practise the missed ideas in Python Lab, and try again.

After reaching 90%, the check is complete. You may continue towards 100% to strengthen your understanding.

Projects and evidence

The foundation assignment checks core Python. The data-analysis assignment checks a guided workflow. The final project asks you to select a question, analyse data, create a chart, and explain the evidence.

content.text:
Responsible AI use

AI tools are allowed for learners and teachers. The goal is better learning, fewer avoidable errors, and less wasted effort—not copying an answer that nobody has checked.

The required workflow

Ask → Read → Run → Check → Modify → Explain.

  • Good uses: ask for a simpler explanation, interpret an error, request a hint, review code you wrote, generate an extra practice problem, or check whether an interpretation missed something.
  • Do not: submit unrun code, use code you cannot explain, accept an analysis without comparing it with the data, or present AI-written explanation as your own work.

AI use declaration for every project

  1. Did you use an AI tool? Yes or No.
  2. What did you ask it to help with?
  3. What did you test, change, or verify yourself?
  4. What did you learn from using it?

Using AI is not a reason to lose marks. Failing to verify or explain the submitted work is.

Estimated study time: 1.5 hours

Learning objectives

  • Run a Python statement
  • Distinguish text, numbers, and expressions
  • Predict simple output

Core idea

A program is a sequence of instructions. print() displays a value. Text is written inside quotes; numbers are not. Python evaluates an expression before printing it.

Worked example

print("Hello, Python!")
print(7 + 5)
print("7 + 5")

The second line prints 12 because Python calculates the expression. The third prints the characters 7 + 5 because they are text.

Practice: type, run, change, explain

  1. Predict all three outputs, then run the code.
  2. Change the greeting and both numbers.
  3. Add one line that multiplies two numbers. Explain the difference between code and output.
AI checkpoint: If you use AI, ask for a hint or explanation first. Run its suggestion, test it with a different value, change at least one part, and be ready to explain it.

Naledi’s next task: Naledi starts by displaying one centre’s monthly registrations and attendance.

Store 40 registered learners and 34 attendees, then print a readable two-line report.

attended = 34

content.text:
Estimated study time: 2 hours

Learning objectives

  • Store and update values
  • Use int, float, and str
  • Convert input before calculating

Core idea

A variable gives a value a useful name. input() always returns text, so numerical input must be converted. Use meaningful names and include units when they matter.

Worked example

name = input("Your name: ")
hours = float(input("Hours studied: "))
days = int(input("Number of days: "))
average = hours / days
print(name, "studied", average, "hours per day")

float accepts a decimal value. int accepts a whole number. The variable names make the calculation readable.

Practice: type, run, change, explain

  1. Run with 10 hours and 5 days.
  2. Test a decimal such as 7.5 hours.
  3. Modify the program to calculate weekly cost from price and quantity.
AI checkpoint: If you use AI, ask for a hint or explanation first. Run its suggestion, test it with a different value, change at least one part, and be ready to explain it.

Naledi’s next task: The coordinator now needs a percentage rather than two separate counts.

Calculate attendance rate for 34 attendees from 40 registered learners and display 85.0%.

attended = 34

print("Attendance rate:", round(attendance_rate, 1), "%")

content.text:
Estimated study time: 2 hours

Learning objectives

  • Compare values
  • Write if/elif/else logic
  • Test boundary cases

Core idea

Conditions choose which block runs. Indentation is part of Python syntax. Boundary values—such as exactly 50—deserve deliberate tests.

Worked example

score = 68
if score >= 70:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 50:
    grade = "Pass"
else:
    grade = "Not yet"
print(grade)

Python checks from top to bottom and stops at the first true condition. With 68, the second condition is true.

Practice: type, run, change, explain

  1. Predict results for 49, 50, 69, and 70.
  2. Add validation for scores below 0 or above 100.
  3. Explain why the order of the conditions matters.
AI checkpoint: If you use AI, ask for a hint or explanation first. Run its suggestion, test it with a different value, change at least one part, and be ready to explain it.

Naledi’s next task: Naledi must flag a centre for support when attendance is below 75%, and watch it from 75% through 84.9%.

Connected worked example

Classify an attendance rate of 72.5 as support, 80 as watch, and 88 as on track.

rate = 72.5
if rate < 75:
    status = "support"
elif rate < 85:
    status = "watch"
else:
    status = "on track"
print(status)
Why this answer works

Run it first, change one input, and connect every output to the named operational measure.

Transfer challenge

Materials below 10 units require reorder; 10–19 require monitoring; 20 or more are sufficient. Test 9, 10, 19, and 20.

The teacher has a reference answer. Your code may differ if it is correct and explainable.

Path to larger data: A boundary error at 75% can misclassify thousands of centre-month records, so test below, at, and above every threshold.

Estimated study time: 2 hours

Learning objectives

  • Iterate through a collection
  • Maintain a running total
  • Recognise a loop boundary

Core idea

A for loop performs the same pattern for each item. An accumulator such as total stores a result that grows during the loop.

Worked example

scores = [62, 74, 81, 55]
total = 0
for score in scores:
    total = total + score
average = total / len(scores)
print(average)

The loop visits every score once. len(scores) is 4, so the final total is divided by 4.

Practice: type, run, change, explain

  1. Trace total after every loop iteration.
  2. Add another score and predict the new average.
  3. Count how many scores are at least 60.
AI checkpoint: If you use AI, ask for a hint or explanation first. Run its suggestion, test it with a different value, change at least one part, and be ready to explain it.

Sum [31, 33, 30, 34] and calculate the weekly mean.

weekly_attendance = [31, 33, 30, 34]
total = 0
for attended in weekly_attendance:
    total += attended
mean = total / len(weekly_attendance)
print("Total:", total)
print("Weekly mean:", mean)

content.text:
When the file no longer feels small

Estimated study time: 3 hours

Learning objectives

  • Estimate whether a file fits in memory
  • Read only needed columns with explicit types
  • Aggregate a CSV in chunks
  • Reconcile chunk results with independent totals

“Big data” is relative to the available computer. The professional habit is to reduce data early, preserve an audit trail, and validate the final totals. Start with file size, columns, types, row count, missingness, and the question you need to answer.

import pandas as pd

totals = {}
row_count = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(
    "transactions.csv",
    usecols=["district", "amount"],
    dtype={"district": "category", "amount": "float64"},
    chunksize=100_000,
):
    row_count += len(chunk)
    part = chunk.groupby("district", observed=True)["amount"].sum()
    for district, amount in part.items():
        totals[district] = totals.get(district, 0) + amount

print("Rows processed:", row_count)
print(totals)

Validation checklist

  1. Compare processed row count with the source expectation.
  2. Count rejected or missing amounts.
  3. Compare the grand total with a second calculation on a small known fixture.
  4. Record file name, date, filters, and cleaning decisions.

Privacy and proportionality

Do not collect personal data merely because storage is available. Remove identifiers not needed for the question, restrict access, and prefer aggregated reporting where possible.

Connection: variables hold running totals; conditions validate rows; loops process chunks; dictionaries merge group results; functions make checks reusable; pandas performs column and group operations; charts communicate the final aggregate.

  • Where are data-quality problems concentrated?

Required workflow

  1. Write the question and data dictionary.
  2. Record size, row count, columns, types, missingness, and privacy decision.
  3. Build and test the analysis on a small fixture.
  4. Run the full data with selected columns/types or chunks where appropriate.
  5. Reconcile row counts, rejected rows, and totals.
  6. Create a decision-sized table and one chart.
  7. State a finding, limitation, and recommended next action.

Submit

  • Runnable code or notebook
  • Small test fixture
  • Cleaning and processing log
  • Summary table and labelled chart
  • 300–500 word decision note

Rubric

  • Question, data understanding, and privacy: 15
  • Test fixture and reproducibility: 15
  • Efficient, correct processing: 25
  • Validation and reconciliation: 15
  • Table, chart, and interpretation: 20
  • Explanation and AI declaration: 10

Required AI use declaration

  1. Did you use an AI tool?
  2. What help did you request?
  3. What did you run, test, change, or verify?
  4. What did you learn?
Read the task, run the example, and explain your decisions.

content.text:
Teacher reference: Scale-up capstone

There is no single required dataset or exact solution. A strong submission demonstrates the following trace:

  1. A small fixture with a manually verifiable result
  2. Explicit usecols, dtype, or justified chunk size
  3. Counts for processed, missing, invalid, and excluded rows
  4. Chunk totals merged correctly across repeated groups
  5. A final aggregate small enough to inspect
  6. A claim supported by numbers, with a limitation and no unsupported causation

Oral modification prompts

  • Change the chunk size. Why should the result remain the same?
  • Add one invalid row to the fixture. Where is it counted?
  • Change a filter threshold and predict the direction of change.
  • Explain one AI suggestion you rejected or modified.

Do not reward sheer row count. Reward correctness, validation, proportional data use, and the learner’s ability to explain and modify the work.

content.text:
Meet Naledi

Naledi supports several community learning centres. She can use files and a browser but has never programmed. Her laptop has limited memory and the internet is not always available.

Every month she receives registration, attendance, completion, teaching-hour, and material-cost records. At first she calculates reports by hand. During this course she will turn that repeated work into a tested Python workflow.

The connected journey

  1. Calculate one centre correctly.
  2. Apply decisions and process several weeks.
  3. Represent several centres and reuse calculations.
  4. Load the same records from CSV.
  5. Clean, group, and visualise them.
  6. Process several years in chunks.
  7. Transfer the method to a licensed open dataset.

Your role: work alongside Naledi. The worked example shows one step. The transfer challenge asks you to use the same idea on a different operational measure.

intro.text: Follow Naledi as the reporting workflow grows one step at a time.

content.text:
Teacher answers: Connected transfer challenges

These are reference approaches, not exact-match requirements. Ask learners to run, modify, and explain their solution.

Lesson 1: Your first Python program

Challenge: A course scheduled 24 training hours and delivered 20. Display both values with clear labels.

Reference: scheduled = 24; delivered = 20; print both values with labels. Accept separate lines or one readable line.

Lesson 2: Variables, types, input, and calculations

Challenge: A centre has 29 completions from 36 registered learners. Calculate its completion percentage to one decimal place.

Reference: 29 / 36 * 100 gives about 80.6%. The learner should identify registered as the denominator.

Lesson 3: Decisions with conditions

Challenge: Materials below 10 units require reorder; 10–19 require monitoring; 20 or more are sufficient. Test 9, 10, 19, and 20.

Reference: Use if stock < 10, elif stock < 20, else. The four boundary tests should produce reorder, monitor, monitor, sufficient.

Lesson 4: Repetition with loops

Challenge: Loop through weekly material costs [82.5, 74.0, 91.5, 80.0] and report total and highest weekly cost.

Reference: The total is 328.0 and the maximum is 91.5. A loop-based maximum or max() is acceptable if explained.

Lesson 5: Lists and dictionaries

Challenge: Add a third centre containing course name, scheduled hours, and delivered hours; print delivery percentage.

Reference: Use one dictionary with labelled keys, append it to the list, then calculate delivered / scheduled * 100.

Lesson 6: Functions, errors, and testing

Challenge: Create cost_per_completion(material_cost, completed) with the same invalid-denominator protection. Test 450/30 and 450/0.

Reference: The valid result is 15.0 and the zero-completion result should be None or another explicitly documented invalid result.

Lesson 7: Tables, CSV, and pandas

Challenge: Select centre_name, registered, and completed, then calculate a completion_rate column.

Reference: Use a column list for selection and df["completed"] / df["registered"] * 100 for the new column.

Lesson 8: Inspecting and selecting data

Challenge: Create a list of centre-months with at least 24 scheduled training hours but fewer than 20 delivered hours.

Reference: Combine both Boolean conditions with &, wrap each in parentheses, and select only identifying and hour columns.

Lesson 9: Cleaning data

Challenge: Flag negative material cost, delivered hours above scheduled hours, and duplicate centre-month-course rows. Report each count.

Reference: Use comparisons for impossible ranges and duplicated(subset=[...], keep=False). Do not silently discard the rows.

Lesson 10: Grouping and summary statistics

Challenge: Group by course and calculate total training hours, total material cost, and cost per completion.

Reference: Aggregate hours, cost, and completions by course, then divide each course total cost by its total completions.

Lesson 11: Visualisation and evidence

Challenge: Create a bar chart comparing completion rate by course. Write one observation and one limitation.

Reference: Aggregate totals before calculating each course rate. A limitation could be differing course difficulty or small group size.

Extension: Transfer the workflow to open data

After the fictional capstone works, repeat the analysis with an openly licensed dataset. “Publicly accessible” does not automatically mean reusable.

Selection checklist

  1. The licence explicitly permits the intended reuse and redistribution, such as CC0 or CC BY.
  2. The source and publisher are identifiable.
  3. The dataset contains no unnecessary personal or sensitive information.
  4. The schema and file version can be recorded.
  5. A local copy can be retained for an offline class.

Required provenance note

  • Dataset title and publisher
  • Direct source URL
  • Licence and attribution text
  • Download date and file checksum
  • Any filtering, renaming, or derived columns

Learning checks: Practise until the ideas are yours

These activities are not one-time examinations. They help you find what you understand, notice a misconception, read an explanation, and try again.

  1. Attempt all ten questions without fear of mistakes.
  2. Submit and read the feedback for every option you missed.
  3. Return to the connected example and run or trace it.
  4. Change one value or boundary.
  5. Try the learning check again. Your highest score is kept.

Progress

  • 90% or more: passed—congratulations.
  • 100%: mastery target.

Some wrong answers are common mistakes on purpose: reversed division, text used as a number, an excluded boundary, AND confused with OR, mean confused with median, or group percentages averaged incorrectly.

content.text:
Analysis toolkit: Boolean logic, sets, and basic statistics

These ideas appear inside Python and pandas rather than as a separate mathematics examination.

Boolean logic

priority = (registered >= 30) and (attendance_rate < 75)
review = missing_data or impossible_value
valid = not duplicate
  • AND: both conditions must be true.
  • OR: at least one condition must be true.
  • NOT: reverses true and false.

Sets

expected = {"Central", "North", "South"}
observed = set(df["district"].dropna())
unexpected = observed - expected
missing = expected - observed

Sets keep unique values. Intersection finds shared values; difference finds values present in one set but not the other.

Basic statistics

  • Count: how many observations.
  • Mean: sum divided by count; sensitive to extreme values.
  • Median: middle ordered value; often more resistant to extremes.
  • Range: maximum minus minimum.
  • Weighted rate: total attended divided by total registered—not usually the simple mean of centre percentages.
weighted_rate = df["attended"].sum() / df["registered"].sum() * 100

A statistic summarises the observed data. It does not by itself establish a cause.

intro.text: Use this reference while practising and reviewing feedback.

content.text:
Teacher guide: Misconception-driven learning checks

The purpose is retrieval practice and feedback, not ranking learners. Permit unlimited attempts and keep the highest score. Ask learners to explain a changed example rather than memorise an option position.

Deliberate distractors

  • Numerator and denominator reversed
  • Boundary excluded by > instead of >=
  • AND and OR confused
  • String concatenation mistaken for addition
  • Row percentages averaged instead of aggregating counts
  • Mean used without checking extreme values or group size
  • Set union confused with intersection
  • Correlation described as causation

If a question has a high error rate, treat it as feedback about instruction. Demonstrate the misconception with small values, then let learners retry.
